author: Delaney Rogers
title: MSU experimental documentary explores modern surveillance - NewsBreak
text:
By Delaney Rogers ,
47 minutes ago EAST LANSING, Mich. (WLNS) — For the past four years, MSU professor and filmmaker Troy Hale has been taking a deeper look at mass surveillance technology. Now, with Flock cameras becoming increasingly common, he thought now was the perfect time to premiere his experimental film "Humanity (1984-2026)."
It's not uncommon to see camera surveillance in everyday life. From dashboard to security cameras to even having one at your fingertips with a smartphone. Over the years, Hale has seen how these devices have become a massive part of daily life.
The screening of "Humanity (1984-2026). (WLNS) "There's cameras everywhere now. You've got them. I've got my glasses. You've got them in your car for your dash cams. You have Ring doorbells. There's security cameras in this building. There's Flock cameras that have AI on them now that track you," Hale said. So, those are a lot of the changes now. Before we would walk around, we weren't really carrying cellphones with cameras all the time."
This is Hale's first art documentary, produced with the help of his students. He says ideas come to him often – when he walks around and sees something, he will add it to a list. The inspiration for Humanity came when Hale began noticing cameras everywhere.
"I was walking through a big box store, and I decided to count the cameras one day and there was 109 cameras in one of these huge stores. And I said, "'Well, why are they there?' They're not just to stop me from stealing some Oreos. No, they're there to track you and your shopping habits."
The screening of "Humanity (1984-2026). (WLNS) Hale says it's meant to explore the relationship between growing camera use and personal privacy. The documentary uses rapid montages and a range of videos from the internet to bring a sense of unease to the audience — an intentional choice made by Hale.
"There's so many cameras watching us that I wanted the audience to feel that there's so many different angles of a certain shot," he said.
The documentary references George Orwell's "1984" — a political, dystopian novel that warns against being mass surveillance.
Michigan State University professor and filmmaker Troy Hale. (WLNS) "It was not meant to be an instruction manual, it was meant to be a warning for us. And that's kind of what has happened now," Hale said. "So that's part of it is, you know, we had this warning about mass surveillance and now we kind of have it."
Hale says with increasing concerns over artificial intelligence-powered license plate readers, it's important to look up and notice the amount of surveillance.
The screening was part of the museum's programming series for "Reality Check," an exhibition that explores how artificial intelligence is shaping the future.
